article.title: Getting Grounded October – Zoning Final Draft Fails Community Gardens and Urban Farms
article.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
article.content: by Elizabeth Henderson Revisions of zoning codes happen at long intervals, so this is a chance for Rochester to make changes that will govern the city for at least the next decade. The process has been underway for over four years and seems to overwhelm the staff which has not met any of their deadlines. In their revisions, the zoning writers have responded to some of the requests from the Food Policy Council and Urban Agriculture Working Group, but we have more work to do. The April 2026 Draft turns out to be their final language. Now it is up to City Council which has the power to make amendments or to accept the draft as is. If you want to support community gardening, please attend one of these sessions and speak up or send in written comments! The zoning revisions process bears the title Zoning Alignment Project because the zoning is supposed to align with the City’s Rochester 2034 Comprehensive Plan . The vision for the plan is lovely: ”Rochester is a beautiful, progressive, lively, healthy, and welcoming city. We build from strength – leveraging our assets to grow our population, local business community, and tax base. We celebrate our 200th birthday in 2034 as a resilient and confident community where diverse neighborhoods are engaged and thriving; downtown is the vibrant heart of our region; our unique network of active waterfronts is accessible to all; and innovation, adaptation, and inclusion drive us forward.” – The People of Rochester In the spirit of this vision, the Food Policy Council prefaced our comments with this reflection: “Community gardens in Rochester are not evenly distributed resources, and they are not evenly burdened by regulation. Taproot Collective’s 2024 – 25 Gardening Together Study – a site survey of 109 Rochester community gardens and qualitative interviews with eight urban growers – documents what planning maps confirm: the gardens that serve Rochester’s most disinvested neighborhoods, often operating on city-permitted vacant lots with no permanent infrastructure, are run predominantly by Black and brown residents with the least margin to absorb bureaucratic cost or legal uncertainty. These are the gardens that a $100 beehive permit fee prices out. These are the gardens that a 144 sq ft greenhouse cap renders non-compliant. And these are the gardeners who have historically been taught to use toxic practices – including tire planters – because those were the cheap materials available to them. “This is the equity dimension of the ZAP that these comments address. The Rochester Food Policy Council – itself supported by Rochester 2034 Action UAG-1i – urges the City Planning Commission to read its urban agriculture provisions not only as technical land use code, but as environmental justice policy. Rochester 2034 (p. 311) identifies local food and urban agriculture as both climate mitigation and adaptation strategies. The Community Food Systems Plan grounds Goal 3 explicitly in equity and calls for making it “easier for residents to grow food where they live,” with particular attention to neighborhoods facing structural barriers including historical disinvestment. In order to be an equitable and efficient policy, the ZAP must align with both documents. Here is a guide to commenting based on the FPC comments: Garden Investment Security: Rochester 2034 calls for long-term land security in multiple action items: VNT-3a, VNT-4d, and UAG-2a collectively direct the City to create 5 – 10-year permit/lease arrangements and to include long-term garden use provisions in the ZAP rewrite. The ZAP does not implement these actions. The equity dimension is acute. Annual revocability is not a neutral administrative feature – it is a structural barrier that falls hardest on lower-income gardeners who cannot risk multi-year investment in infrastructure on land that can be taken back at any time. The newly released Rochester Community Food System Plan (CFSP) reinforces this finding, noting that land tenure insecurity “discourages long-term investment and planning from gardeners” and that gardeners in disinvested neighborhoods have explicitly called for relief from “complicated communication and processes, uncertain land tenure, and perceived lack of support” (CFSP p. 109). The ZAP should classify gardens as permitted in all residential neighborhoods. Recommendation: To align with Rochester 2034, the city should adopt zoning that clusters development more densely along transit corridors. The city can then designate vacant lots that are not on these corridors for use as greenspace and gardens. Each quadrant should get some. Half the city’s 5000 vacant lots are city property which it spends $260 a piece each year to keep “clean and green.” The city saves money when residents take over. When the city permits residents to use its lots for gardens, those lots can be divided into two distinct categories and clearly labeled as reserved for future development or reserved for use as gardens, farms or green space. The ZGEIS recognizes the distinction, stating: “This use is intended to support nearby residents, so allowing them in residential districts makes sense. Lots reserved for community gardens, as the principal use, would not meet the vision for development along the mixed-use corridors.” But does not take the further step to confirm the value of gardens as a principal use in residential districts. Limitations on Season Extension: Rochester 2034 (p. 311) identifies local food and urban agriculture as both climate mitigation and adaptation strategies. The Community Food Systems Plan grounds Goal 3 explicitly in equity and calls for making it “easier for residents to grow food where they live,” with particular attention to neighborhoods facing structural barriers including historical disinvestment. In order to be an equitable and efficient policy, the ZAP must align with both documents. Rochester 2034 Action UAG-3c explicitly directs the City to “explore support for installation of high tunnels, hoop houses, and other season-extending production aids on City-owned and private land.” The ZAP – which Article 1.2.B requires to implement Rochester 2034 – instead caps community garden greenhouses at 144 square feet and applies a 50% lot-area ceiling to all tunnel structures, treating temporary row covers identically to semi-permanent high tunnels. With climate change, in the Northeast rains are more frequent and come down much harder. Using high tunnels is a way to protect crops from pounding rain, so gardeners or urban farmers might justifiably want to cover as much as 75% of their land in order to have a crop. The April 2026 draft changed the previous limit of 25% to 50%. That is better, but we can ask for more, especially since gardeners might also want to cover 100% of the garden with row covers for a few nights to protect from frost. Recommendation: • Replace the 144 sq ft cap with a lot-coverage percentage, consistent with every peer city reviewed and with UAG-3c. • Clarify Section 14.1.G application to garden lots without principal structures. • Establish grandfathering for existing non-compliant structures. • Create separate standards for high tunnels (permanent/semi-permanent) and low tunnels/row covers (temporary). • Exempt low tunnels and row covers from area calculations entirely. Excessive Fee for Keeping Bees – Recommendation : • Reduce or waive the $100 fee for community garden and urban farm apiaries, particularly those operated by nonprofits or serving low-income populations. • Retain the Section 14.2.B siting standards as written. • Affirm NYS requirement for beekeepers to register their hives with the New York State Department of Agriculture and Markets (https://agriculture.ny.gov/plant-industry/honey-bee-health). • Collaborate with community partners to deliver beekeeping education as part of the permitting process for community gardens and urban farms. Remove Confusion about Garden Beds, Paths and Weeds: Section 16.2.F – General Landscape Requirement requires all non-structure, non-paved lot area to be landscaped with trees, shrubs, live groundcover, and other plantings. Community garden growing beds, mulched paths, and production areas are functional green infrastructure under Rochester 2034’s own framework (UAG p. 321, Vacant Lands p. 171). The FPC requests explicit clarification that these satisfy Section 16.2.F. The equity dimension: any ambiguity in this provision creates enforcement exposure for gardens that are least likely to have legal counsel to navigate it. Clear, affirmative language is needed. Recommendation: • Add explicit language that growing beds, production areas, mulched paths, and other functional garden features satisfy Section 16.2.F for lots used as community gardens or urban farms. Definition of Weeds Needed, Section 16.2.E.2 – Maintenance: Definition of “Weeds” – Recommendation : • Define “weed” in Article 24 to exclude intentionally cultivated native plants, food crops, cover crops, and ecologically functional vegetation. • Add language to Section 16.2.E.2 clarifying that the standard does not apply to intentional plantings in community gardens serving food production, cultural preservation, pollinator support, or ecological function. Reduce Toxics in Landscaping: The ZAP section on landscaping (Section 16 Landscape ) offers the opportunity to limit the use of toxic herbicides and pesticides in the city. There is extensive research on the environmental injustice that low-income people are exposed to significantly more toxics in their living environment than wealthier people. Lead paint, dust, contamination from incinerators and factories are located deliberately in neighborhoods where residents have fewer resources to defend themselves. Section E, on maintenance states: “All landscaping must be maintained free from disease, pests, weeds, and litter.” This is the place to insert – “without the use of carcinogenic or endocrine-disrupting herbicides or pesticides.” The Monroe County Parks including city parks, and the Monroe County Forestry Plan, already have strict limits on the use of toxics only for invasive species or serious diseases. Zoning could hold all landowners to these good practices. City Council Public Hearings: Each of the Rochester City Council District representatives – Vice President LaShay D. Harris (South), Michael A. Patterson (Northeast), Mary Lupien (East) and Bridget A. Monroe (Northwest) – will host an initial public, district meeting in the coming weeks regarding the ZAP legislation currently before City Council. These meetings will be held in each respective Councilmember’s district, and will offer residents an opportunity to voice their opinion on ZAP. Additional meetings will be scheduled as well. No registration is required to attend any of these hearings regardless of where you live. Specific dates and times for the initial District Meetings are as follows: Council Member Michael Patterson (Northeast District): Sept. 29: Rochester Public Market at 5:30pm Sept. 30: Ibero Community Room Council Member Mary Lupien (East District): Oct. 13: Ryan R-Center at 6:00pm Council Member Bridget Monroe (Northwest District): Sept. 28: Edgerton R-Center at 6:00pm Oct. 7: Roback Community Center at 6:00pm Council Member LaShay Harris (South District): Oct. 5: New Life Fellowship at 6:00pm Oct. 14: Olmstead Lodge in Highland Park at 6:00pm Following these initial District Meetings, City Council will host official public hearings with the Evans Administration on Oct. 21 and 22 from 5:00pm – 8:00pm in City Council Chambers. These hearings will be open to attendance by the public and available on the City Council YouTube Channel for those who cannot attend in person. City residents who are unable to make any of the many public meetings can email Council@CityofRochester.Gov , fax (585) 428-6347 or attend City Council’s regular Speak to Council and Public Hearing session on Nov. 12 at 6:00pm. The work session will be held on Oct. 8 in City Hall Room 208A. For more information on the City Council ZAP process, City residents can call the City Council office at (585) 428-7538 or email Council@CityofRochester.Gov . Save this date: the 2027 Rochester Urban Farming Conference will take place Saturday, March 13 from 9:30am – 4:00pm at East High!
